title: Krishna walks into the arena
hook: one Krishna, a whole arena, and everyone sees someone different
carry: the world is real; the mind adds the color

segments.voice: Mathura, the day of King Kamsa's wrestling match. The whole city is packed into the arena. Then two young cowherds walk in from the gate: Krishna and his brother Balarama. The Bhagavata Purana stops the story right there and looks at the crowd. To the wrestlers, Krishna is a thunderbolt. To the men, the finest of men. To the women, love itself, walking. To the cowherds, their own boy. To wicked kings, the one who'll punish them. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. And to Kamsa, up on his platform, he is death.
screen: `ONE BOY WALKS INTO THE ARENA.` → `THE WRESTLERS SEE A THUNDERBOLT.` → `HIS PARENTS SEE THEIR CHILD.` → `KAMSA SEES HIS DEATH.`

segments.voice: One Krishna. A whole arena. A different Krishna in every mind. The Bhagavata isn't a philosophy book, but it paints exactly what Patanjali argues in sutra 4.15: vastusamye chittabhedat tayor vibhaktah panthah. The thing being the same, because the minds differ, the two go separate ways. Vastu is the real thing out there; chitta is the mind. Notice what Patanjali doesn't say. He doesn't say Krishna is ten things, or nothing, or only a picture in each head. Krishna is really there, walking in. The difference is in the minds. And 4.17 says how: a thing is known when the mind takes on its color. Picture a clear glass set on red cloth. Many teachers read the arena this way: Kamsa's mind is colored by fear, so he sees death. His parents' minds are colored by love, so they see a child. Hindu schools argued about this for centuries. Some Buddhist philosophers of the time held that objects are built by the mind, and the old commentary on these sutras answers them; later, Advaita Vedanta would speak of the world as maya. Yoga, with its sister school Samkhya, takes a plain stand: the world is real. So the trouble was never the world. It's the coloring: the craving and the dread the mind lays on it. Yoga doesn't ask you to deny the chair or the cup or your brother. It asks you to clean the glass. You've seen the small version. In 2015, one photo of a dress split the internet: blue and black, or white and gold. Two siblings remember the same family dinner as a disaster and a delight. Same dress. Same dinner. Different glass.
screen: `ONE KRISHNA, MANY MINDS.` · `4.17: THE MIND TAKES ITS COLOR.` · `FEAR SEES DEATH. LOVE SEES A CHILD.` · `YOGA: THE WORLD IS REAL.` · then, large: `THE WORLD IS REAL; THE MIND ADDS THE COLOR.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object near you, a cup, a chair, a plant, and notice the colors your mind lays on it: I like this, this needs washing, someone gave me this. Name each one softly and set it aside. Then let the thing just be there, as itself.
Vastu, the real object out there. For Patanjali, the world is real; minds differ in how they are colored by it.
Your line: the world is real; the mind adds the color. Kamsa saw death; his parents saw a child. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Classical Yoga, like Samkhya, is taught as a realist philosophy: the world of nature is real, and practice aims at freeing the mind from the coloring it takes on, not at denying the world. The Bhagavata's arena verse pictures the same idea: one Krishna, seen by each mind in its own way.

chat.meaning: In the Bhagavata, one Krishna walks into Kamsa's arena and each crowd sees him differently. Sutra 4.15: the thing is the same, the minds differ. For Yoga the world is real; the coloring is in the mind.
